CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3 · JANUARY

Functions and their properties

Mia’s way to school, the temperature over the course of a day, the price of a pizza with extra toppings: everywhere one quantity depends on another. If exactly one other value belongs to every value, we speak of a function. You will learn to represent functions in words, tables, graphs and equations and to read off their properties from the graph.

8 LESSONS2 UNITSREADING GRAPHSMEDIA
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • recognise a function as a unique assignment and check it with the vertical line test
  • represent functions in words, as a table of values, as a graph and as an equation
  • find the domain and the range
  • recognise monotonicity, zeros, maxima and minima and symmetry from the graph

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1What is a function?

At every moment on Mia’s way to school there is exactly one distance from home. The other way round this is not true: while Mia waits at the bus stop, the distance 400 m belongs to many moments. The assignment “time ↦ distance” is a function, the assignment “distance ↦ time” is not.

For a function, $x$ is called the independent variable and $y$ the dependent one. You write $f(x)$ for the value that the function $f$ assigns to $x$. A function can be described in words, as a table of values, as a graph or as an equation. All four representations tell the same story.

KEY POINT · FUNCTION

A function assigns exactly one $y$ to every $x$ from a set.

Notation: $f\colon x \mapsto 2x^3 - 4x$ (mapping rule) or $y = f(x) = 2x^3 - 4x$ (equation of the function). $f(2) = 8$ is the function value at $2$.

Representations: in words, as a table of values, as a graph, as an equation.

Vertical line test: a curve is the graph of a function exactly when every vertical line meets it at most once.

History: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz already used the word functio in the 17th century. Leonhard Euler introduced the notation $f(x)$ in 1734.

Law of distance and time: if you ride steadily at 5 metres per second, you cover $s = 5t$ metres in $t$ seconds. That is a function too.

INTERACTIVE · MIA’S WAY TO SCHOOL

Move the time. The point on the graph and Mia on her way move together. Where is the graph horizontal, where is it steepest?

INTERACTIVE · FUNCTION OR NOT?
EXAMPLE 1 · FOUR REPRESENTATIONS

A pizza costs €7, each extra topping €1.50. Represent the price as an equation and as a table of values for 0 to 4 toppings.

Equation: $p(b) = 7 + 1.5b$ with $b$ = number of toppings, $p$ in euros.

$b$01234
$p(b)$78.501011.5013

In the graph these are separate points. There are no half toppings, so you do not join them.

EXAMPLE 2 · UNIQUE?

Function or not? a) to every person their date of birth   b) to every date the people whose birthday it is   c) to every number its square   d) to every positive number the numbers whose square it is

a) yes, everyone has exactly one date of birth   b) no, often several people or nobody belong to a date

c) yes   d) no: $2$ and $-2$ both belong to $4$.

EXERCISES

Read from Mia’s distance-time graph: a) How far has she got after 4 minutes? b) When is she 2000 m from home? c) How long does she wait at the bus stop?

a) $4 \cdot 80 = 320$ m   b) on the bus: $400 + 300(t - 8) = 2000$, so after about $13.3$ min   c) from minute 5 to 8, so 3 minutes

You are given $f(x) = 2x^3 - 4x$. Calculate $f(0)$, $f(1)$ and $f(-2)$.

$f(0) = 0$, $\;f(1) = 2 - 4 = -2$, $\;f(-2) = -16 + 8 = -8$

A mobile phone contract costs €5 a month and €0.10 per text message. Represent the cost as an equation, as a table of values (0 to 50 texts in steps of ten) and as a graph.

$k(n) = 5 + 0.1n$. Table: 5; 6; 7; 8; 9; 10 euros. The graph consists of points on a line that starts at €5.

Which tables of values belong to a function of $x$? a) $x$: 1, 2, 3, 2 and $y$: 5, 6, 7, 8   b) $x$: 1, 2, 3, 4 and $y$: 5, 5, 5, 5   c) $x$: −1, 0, 1, 2 and $y$: 1, 0, 1, 4

a) no, 6 and 8 both belong to $x = 2$   b) yes, a constant function   c) yes, $y = x^2$. Two values of $x$ having the same $y$ is allowed.

Jonas cycles 3 km to a friend’s house in 10 minutes, stays 20 minutes and then cycles back in 15 minutes. Draw the graph “time ↦ distance from home”. How fast is he on the way there and on the way back?

The graph rises up to $(10, 3)$, is horizontal until minute 30 and falls to $(45, 0)$. Way there: 3 km in 10 min, so 18 km/h. Way back: 3 km in 15 min, so 12 km/h.

$16 - 8$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Properties of functions

The graph of $f(x) = \tfrac12 x^2 - 2$ falls to the left of the origin and rises to the right of it. At the very bottom is the minimum point $T(0, -2)$. It cuts the x-axis at $-2$ and at $2$, and it is symmetrical about the y-axis. You can read all of this directly from the graph.

KEY POINT · PROPERTIES

Domain $D$: all $x$ that may be substituted. For $f(x) = \tfrac1x$, $x = 0$ is forbidden. Range $W$: all $y$ that occur as a function value.

Monotonically increasing: the larger $x$, the larger $f(x)$. Monotonically decreasing: the other way round.

Zero: an $x$ with $f(x) = 0$. There the graph cuts the x-axis. The intersection with the y-axis is given by $f(0)$.

Extrema: maximum points and minimum points, the highest and lowest points in their neighbourhood.

Symmetry: about the y-axis if $f(-x) = f(x)$; about the origin if $f(-x) = -f(x)$.

“The more … the more” with care: “The more ice cream is sold, the more sunburn there is.” That describes a connection, but not a cause. Both depend on the sunshine.

$\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{R}$? The tool below shows $\mathbb{R}$, the real numbers from Year 9. Until then, read it as “all numbers”.

INTERACTIVE · FUNCTION DETECTIVE

Choose a function, think about its properties and then reveal them one by one. For Year 8, $x^2$, $x^3$, $\tfrac1x$, $|x|$ and $\tfrac12 x^2 - 2$ are important, you will get to know the others later.

EXAMPLE 3 · READING FROM THE GRAPH

Read from the graph of $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$: zeros, maximum and minimum point, monotonicity and symmetry.

Zeros at about $-1.7$, at $0$ and at about $1.7$. Maximum point $H(-1, 2)$, minimum point $T(1, -2)$.

Increasing for $x \le -1$ and for $x \ge 1$, decreasing in between. Point-symmetrical about the origin: $f(-x) = -x^3 + 3x = -f(x)$.

EXAMPLE 4 · DOMAIN AND RANGE

Give $D$ and $W$: a) $f(x) = 2x + 1$   b) $g(x) = x^2$   c) $h(x) = \tfrac{1}{x - 2}$

a) $D$ and $W$: all numbers   b) $D$: all numbers, $W$: all $y \ge 0$

c) $D$: all numbers except $2$, there the denominator would be $0$. $W$: all numbers except $0$, because a fraction with numerator $1$ is never $0$.

EXERCISES

Calculate the zeros and the intersection with the y-axis: a) $f(x) = 2x - 6$   b) $g(x) = -x + 4$   c) $h(x) = x^2 - 9$

a) $x = 3$; $(0, -6)$   b) $x = 4$; $(0, 4)$   c) $x = 3$ and $x = -3$; $(0, -9)$

Use $f(-x)$ to check for symmetry: a) $f(x) = x^2 + 1$   b) $g(x) = x^3$   c) $h(x) = x^2 + x$

a) $f(-x) = x^2 + 1 = f(x)$: about the y-axis   b) $g(-x) = -x^3 = -g(x)$: about the origin   c) $h(-x) = x^2 - x$: neither

Sketch the graph of a function with these properties: all numbers may be substituted, zeros at $-2$ and $3$, a maximum point at $x = 0.5$, no other extrema.

An arch opening downwards through $(-2, 0)$ and $(3, 0)$ with its highest point above $x = 0.5$, for example $f(x) = -(x + 2)(x - 3)$.

On a summer’s day it is 14 °C at 6 o’clock. By 15:00 the temperature rises to 29 °C, by midnight it falls to 18 °C. Describe the monotonicity and the extrema of the function “time of day ↦ temperature” from 6:00 to midnight.

Increasing from 6:00 to 15:00, decreasing from 15:00 to midnight. Highest value 29 °C at 15:00, lowest 14 °C at 6:00.

Justify: a function that is point-symmetrical about the origin and defined at $x = 0$ always has the zero $0$.

From $f(-x) = -f(x)$ it follows for $x = 0$ that $f(0) = -f(0)$, so $2f(0) = 0$ and $f(0) = 0$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Zero of $f(x) = 2x - 6$?

$2x = 6$

y-coordinate of the maximum point of $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$?

$f(-1) = -1 + 3$

How is the graph of $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ symmetrical?

$f(-x) = f(x)$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Fill in the table of values for $f\colon x \mapsto x^2 - 2x$ from $x = -1$ to $x = 3$ and draw the graph. Read off the zeros and the minimum point.

Values: 3; 0; −1; 0; 3. Zeros at 0 and 2, minimum point $T(1, -1)$.

A newspaper shows the number of passengers on a tram line over a working day as a curve. Which maxima and minima do you expect? Why is the smooth curve actually a simplification?

Maxima in the rush hours in the morning and the afternoon, a minimum at night. Passengers are counted in whole numbers and usually per quarter of an hour or per hour: really they are bars, the curve smooths them.

Show that the graph of $f(x) = \tfrac1x$ is point-symmetrical about the origin. Why does $f$ have no zero?

$f(-x) = \tfrac{1}{-x} = -\tfrac1x = -f(x)$. A fraction is $0$ only if its numerator is $0$, and here the numerator is always $1$.

Connecting with learning area 2: assign its probability to every total of two dice. Is this a function? Give the domain, the range and the maximum. What symmetry does the graph have?

Yes. $D = \{2, 3, \ldots, 12\}$, $W = \{\tfrac{1}{36}, \tfrac{2}{36}, \ldots, \tfrac{6}{36}\}$. Maximum $\tfrac16$ for the total 7. The graph is symmetrical about the vertical line $x = 7$.

EXCURSIONAPPLICATION

The timetable as a graph

In the 1840s the French railway engineer Charles Ibry invented a timetable to look at. The time of day runs horizontally, the stations stand vertically, at their correct distances. Every train is a line, that is a distance-time graph like Mia’s way to school.

The steeper a line, the faster the train. Horizontal pieces are stops at a station. Where two lines cross, two trains meet, and on a single-track line that may only happen at a station. A picture like this became famous in 1878 through the book La méthode graphique by the physiologist Étienne-Jules Marey.

Graphic timetables like these still help railways today when they plan their timetables.

Source: É.-J. Marey: La méthode graphique dans les sciences expérimentales. Paris 1878.
